analysis.one_liner: Freezes the minimum wage for foreign guest farmworkers at 2021 levels through 2022.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced November 2, 2021 with four Republican cosponsors, it sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have frozen the "adverse effect wage rate" — the minimum wage the government requires farms to pay H-2A guest workers — at its October 2021 level through the end of 2022. The freeze would apply automatically in any state with unemployment of 5% or less in August 2021, or in any state where food prices rose more than 3% between December 2020 and September 2021 if that state's governor requested it. The stated aim was to hold down food prices; the actual effect would have been to keep farm employers' labor costs down by blocking a scheduled raise for some of the lowest-paid workers in the country.
analysis.who_benefits: Farm operators and growers who hire H-2A guest workers would benefit, because they would avoid the wage increase the Labor Department had scheduled for 2022 and keep paying their workers at the lower 2021 rate for another year. Agricultural lobby groups had been pushing for exactly this kind of relief as the adverse effect wage rate climbed. Because the adverse effect wage rate also acts as a wage floor that influences what farms pay their whole workforce in many states, employers could hold down labor costs beyond just their guest workers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Farms that hire H-2A guest workers

how_it_helps.text: It freezes the adverse effect wage rate — the required minimum wage for H-2A guest farmworkers — at its October 1, 2021 level through December 31, 2022, so farm employers would avoid paying the higher 2022 rate the Labor Department had set.

The freeze is written to cover nearly every state automatically: it applies in any state with unemployment of 5% or less in August 2021, or in any state where the food price index rose more than 3% between December 2020 and September 2021 if the governor asks for it — conditions that would have captured most of the country in 2021.

Because the H-2A minimum wage must also be at least as high as the adverse effect wage rate, prevailing rate, federal minimum, or state minimum, holding the adverse effect wage rate down holds down the wage floor that farm employers pay across their workforce.

analysis.who_pays: H-2A guest workers and, by extension, other farmworkers: their wage floor would be frozen while consumer prices and food prices were rising, meaning a real pay cut for workers who are typically among the lowest-paid in the country. Consumers would see little of the promised food-price relief, since farm labor is a small share of what a grocery item costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Guest farmworkers and low-wage farm labor

drawbacks.text: Freezing the wage floor through 2022, a year of rapid inflation, would have meant a real pay cut for H-2A workers and the farmworkers whose wages track the adverse effect wage rate — the very people the bill's title says it is trying to help with 'affordable' food.

The food-price justification is thin: farm labor is only a small slice of the retail cost of food, so even a meaningful wage freeze for guest workers would barely move grocery prices, while the wage savings would flow to farm employers.

A good-faith concern from the other side is real and was the bill's premise: growers argued that rapidly rising adverse effect wage rates were squeezing farm margins and raising food costs, and the bill was the industry's vehicle for relief.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit — one year of lower labor costs for farms that hire guest workers — is real but narrow, and its cost lands on workers already near the bottom of the wage scale precisely when inflation was eroding their paychecks. Its headline promise of stabilizing food prices is out of proportion to the mechanism, since farm wages are a small part of retail food prices. On balance it is a wage freeze for vulnerable workers dressed up as consumer relief.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or vote, so the bill expired when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Tillis introduced the bill on November 2, 2021, joined by Senators Boozman, Cornyn, and Graham as cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee — the committee that handles H-2A visa law — and no further action was ever taken.
The bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the 2021 wage freeze was never enacted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Farmworkers come out ahead: the adverse effect wage rate kept rising as scheduled, so guest workers and the broader farm labor market kept the higher wage floor instead of having it frozen during inflation. Farm employers who wanted the freeze got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Farmworkers, whose wage floor kept rising

for.name: Sen. Thom Tillis
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to freeze the H-2A adverse effect wage rate through 2022.

for.name: Sens. John Boozman, John Cornyn, and Lindsey Graham
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; 4 of 50 Senate Republicans signed on.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (Chair Dick Durbin)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over H-2A visa law
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after its November 2, 2021 referral, letting it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors were Republicans (4 of 50 Senate Republicans), but the bill never came to a vote in committee or on the floor, so no roll-call record shows where the parties stood.

industries.industry: Farms and growers that hire H-2A guest workers
industries.note: The bill would have saved these employers a year of scheduled wage increases by freezing the required minimum wage for guest workers. It never passed, so they did not get the relief; their gain would have come directly out of farmworkers' pay.

industries.industry: Agricultural labor contractors and H-2A recruiters
industries.note: These intermediaries bill by the wage rate, so a frozen wage would have meant smaller contracts, but their business model was untouched either way. The bill died, so nothing changed for them.
